catalog_quote: Stress is marked sporadically in the MS, but where marked, it is invariably on the first syllable with a consonantal onset. Laves uses either a straight apostrophe preceding the syllable or an acute accent mark on the vowel to indicate stress; I have reproduced these marks literally in the examples below. Athima is an initial-dropping language: abmal 'foot' < Proto-Paman *tjamal. In some cases Laves has written an initial "y" before /i/ where one would expect the /i/ to be initial on historical grounds: yidna 'ear' (< Proto-Paman *pina, with idna the expected reflex). ... Laves also heard initial [w] for at least some forms that probably begin with /u/, as with wub'man 'lower leg' (< Proto-Paman *kuman)—it is significant here that Laves marked stress on the second syllable. Note also 'wub'mu 'nose', with stress marked for the second syllable as well as the first (I do not know of a cognate for this form, with or without initial consonant). ... I consider /bm/ and /dn/ to be unit phonemes (prestopped nasals) of the type found in a number of languages of this area, despite Laves' rendition of them (to judge from the stress mark written between the stop symbol and the nasal symbol) as split between two syllables.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Where Laves marked stress at all, it falls on the first syllable that has a consonant onset. Because Athima is an initial-dropping language whose words are (almost all) vowel-initial, that is the second syllable of the word: ab'mal 'foot', a'madhv 'lower leg', a'thaba 'elder sister', a'thigv 'mother's brother', i'wetin 'mouth', i'yin 'father's sister', yid'na (= /idna/) 'ear', ur'dum 'belly', a'pandvl 'chin'. Alpher treats the y-/w-initial transcriptions as Laves' artifacts (yidna = /idna/, wub'man = /ubman/), so the second-syllable stress marked on those forms fits the same rule; only 'wub'mu 'nose' carries a mark on both syllables. This matches the non-initial stress of the closest relatives (Sommer 1969 on Kunjen: disyllables stressed finally). An alternative coding faithful to Alpher's wording is 'fixed: other position: first onset-bearing syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. One form, 'wub'mu 'nose', is marked for stress on both syllables; Alpher offers no analysis beyond noting it.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is marked only sporadically in the 1931 manuscript; no exceptions to the rule are stated other than the double-marked 'wub'mu. Alpher warns that Laves' transcription shows interference from 'other Australian languages of a more usual phonological type' (consonant-initial), and that the whole corpus is about 55 lexical items and 19 elicited sentences.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, as recorded in isolated words and short elicited sentences in Laves' 1931 wordlist from a single speaker (Jack Munsel, Normanton). Alpher reproduces Laves' stress marks (apostrophe before the syllable or acute accent) literally in the wordlist (pp. 4-8). Not an instrumental or fieldwork-based phonological study; the language is extinct and no other data exist.
new_statements.identity_note: Athima = Glottolog athi1234 = AUSTLANG Y237 (AIATSIS reference name 'Athina'; Wikidata alias 'Athina'); no ISO code. The language is known solely from Gerhardt Laves' 1931 notes (Alpher's PDF says 1931; Alpher's 2016 bibliography says 1930) from one speaker, Jack Munsel, taken 'probably in Normanton' with the heading 'Normanton—Gilbert River'; the name is recorded in the list itself as a'thimv. Alpher surmises the country lies on the middle reaches of the Gilbert River; its closest relative is Ogunyjan (Kawarrang-Ogh Undjan, kawa1290; 59% shared vocabulary in the list), and Wikipedia treats it as 'a fifth variety' of Kunjen (kunj1245). Glottolog and AUSTLANG treat it as a separate language within Southwestern Alaya-Athima. Not covered by Sommer 1969's Kunjen dialects (Oykangand, Olgol, Okunjan, Kawarrangg).
